Answer ALL questions; each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D and only one answer must be marked (if more than one answer is marked the score for that question is zero). Mathematical tables (formulae booklets) and calculators are allowed. Section A: Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35); Section B: Mechanics (questions 36 to 50). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

$\dfrac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $\dfrac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+2}$ and multiply through by $(x-1)(x+2)$: $5x+1\equiv A(x+2)+B(x-1)$. Put $x=1$: $6=3A$, so $A=2$. Put $x=-2$: $-9=-3B$, so $B=3$. Check: $2(x+2)+3(x-1)=5x+1$. So the expression is $\dfrac{2}{x-1}+\dfrac{3}{x+2}$. Option A has the wrong value $B=2$; options B and D (printed identically) have a sign error in $B$ (a sign error when solving for $B$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equations of the vertical asymptotes to the graph of $f(x)=\dfrac{4}{x^2-1}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not. Here $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)=0$ gives $x=1$ and $x=-1$, and the numerator $4$ is never zero. So the vertical asymptotes are $x=1$ and $x=-1$ (the horizontal asymptote is $y=0$). The value $4$ in options A, B and D is the numerator, which has nothing to do with asymptotes. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=x-2$. The composite function $gf=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The composite $gf$ means apply $f$ first, then $g$: $gf(x)=g(f(x))=f(x)-2=(2x+3)-2=2x+1$. Option B, $2x-1$, is the composite in the other order: $fg(x)=f(x-2)=2(x-2)+3=2x-1$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If $\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&9\end{pmatrix}$, then the cofactor of the element $6$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$   B) $\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$   C) $-\begin{vmatrix}-1&-2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$   D) $\begin{vmatrix}-1&-2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The element $6$ is in row $2$, column $3$. Its cofactor is $C_{23}=(-1)^{2+3}M_{23}$, where the minor $M_{23}$ is the determinant left when row $2$ and column $3$ are deleted, namely $\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}=8-14=-6$. So $C_{23}=-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}=-(-6)=6$, which is option A in standard form. Option B is the minor without the sign $(-1)^{2+3}$, with value $-6$. Option C has value $-(-8+14)=-6$. Option D, however, also has the value $-8+14=6$ (negating a row negates a determinant, so it equals option A numerically), so the printed question has two options equal to the cofactor $6$.

**Intended answer: A ($-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $4^{2-x}=4\left(2^{1-x}\right)$, the value of $x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Write both sides with base $2$: $4^{2-x}=2^{2(2-x)}=2^{4-2x}$ and $4\left(2^{1-x}\right)=2^2\cdot2^{1-x}=2^{3-x}$. Equal powers of $2$ give equal exponents: $4-2x=3-x$, so $x=1$. Check: $4^{1}=4$ and $4\cdot2^{0}=4$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\ln(x+6)+\ln 9=\ln(x+7)+\ln 6$, the value of $x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\ln a+\ln b=\ln(ab)$ on both sides: $\ln\big(9(x+6)\big)=\ln\big(6(x+7)\big)$. Since $\ln$ is one-to-one, $9(x+6)=6(x+7)$, so $9x+54=6x+42$, $3x=-12$ and $x=-4$. Check: $x+6=2>0$ and $x+7=3>0$, and $\ln 2+\ln 9=\ln 18=\ln 3+\ln 6$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the roots of the quadratic equation $px^2-qx-r=0$ are real, then
questions.corrige_markdown: The roots are real (equal or distinct) exactly when the discriminant is non-negative. Here $a=p$, $b=-q$, $c=-r$, so $b^2-4ac=q^2-4p(-r)=q^2+4pr\ge0$. Option A forgets that $c=-r$; option D has the wrong sign and a strict inequality (distinct roots only); option C is not a discriminant condition. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\dfrac{2}{3n}\right)^n=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\dfrac{c}{n}\right)^n=e^{c}$ with $c=\dfrac23$ (write $\dfrac{2}{3n}=\dfrac{2/3}{n}$). The limit is $e^{2/3}$. Numerical check: for $n=10^7$ the expression is $1.947734\ldots$ and $e^{2/3}=1.947734\ldots$. Option A inverts the exponent. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given two statements $p$ and $q$, the converse of $p\Rightarrow q$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The converse of an implication $p\Rightarrow q$ swaps hypothesis and conclusion: $q\Rightarrow p$. (The contrapositive would be $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$ and the inverse $\sim p\Rightarrow\sim q$; option D is neither of these.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The ordered pair that satisfies the following simultaneous equations is $2x+3y=1$, $3x-y=7$.
questions.corrige_markdown: From $3x-y=7$ we get $y=3x-7$. Substitute into $2x+3y=1$: $2x+9x-21=1$, so $11x=22$ and $x=2$, hence $y=3(2)-7=-1$. Check in both equations: $2(2)+3(-1)=1$ and $3(2)-(-1)=7$. The pair is $(2,-1)$. The other pairs fail at least one equation, for example $(2,1)$ gives $2x+3y=7$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $1-\cos x=2\sin^2\dfrac x2$, we get $\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x}=\sin\dfrac x2\cdot\dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\to0\cdot1=0$. Alternatively, L'Hopital's rule gives $\dfrac{\sin x}{1}\to0$. The value $1$ would be the limit of $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$, and $\dfrac12$ the limit of $\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}$; neither is the limit asked. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Using the substitution $u=1+x^2$, $\displaystyle\int_0^1 2x(1+x^2)^3\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: With $u=1+x^2$, $du=2x\,dx$. The limits change: $x=0\Rightarrow u=1$ and $x=1\Rightarrow u=2$. So $\displaystyle\int_0^1 2x(1+x^2)^3\,dx=\int_1^2u^3\,du=\left[\dfrac{u^4}{4}\right]_1^2=\dfrac{16}{4}-\dfrac14=\dfrac{15}{4}$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x+1}{2x}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Split the fraction: $\dfrac{2x+1}{2x}=1+\dfrac{1}{2x}$. Then $\displaystyle\int\left(1+\dfrac{1}{2x}\right)dx=x+\dfrac12\ln|x|+K$. Check by differentiating: $1+\dfrac{1}{2x}$. Options C and D put a factor $2$ in front of the logarithm instead of $\dfrac12$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Using De Moivre's theorem, the complex number $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^5$ is equal to
questions.corrige_markdown: De Moivre's theorem states that $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$. With $n=5$ the result is $\cos5\theta+i\sin5\theta$. Option A raises the angle (not the number) to the power $5$, and option D is the fifth root (angle divided by $5$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are coplanar vectors, where $\mathbf u=2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+6\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf v=-3\mathbf i+5\mathbf j+\mathbf k$, $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2&-1&6\\-3&5&1\end{vmatrix}=\mathbf i\big((-1)(1)-6\cdot5\big)-\mathbf j\big(2\cdot1-6\cdot(-3)\big)+\mathbf k\big(2\cdot5-(-1)(-3)\big)=-31\mathbf i-20\mathbf j+7\mathbf k$. Check: the result must be perpendicular to both vectors: $2(-31)-1(-20)+6(7)=-62+20+42=0$ and $-3(-31)+5(-20)+1(7)=93-100+7=0$. Option B forgets the minus sign in front of the $\mathbf j$ term. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f(x)$ is continuous in the interval $[a,b]$ and differentiable on the interval $(a,b)$. The mean value theorem states that there exists a value $c$, where $a<c<b$, such that
questions.corrige_markdown: The mean value theorem says that somewhere strictly between $a$ and $b$ the tangent is parallel to the chord joining $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$. The chord has gradient $\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, so $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. Options C and D involve $f'(a)$ and $f'(b)$ (values of the derivative at the ends), and option A adds the function values. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The tangent of the acute angle between the lines $y=4x-3$ and $y=x-2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The gradients are $m_1=4$ and $m_2=1$. The tangent of the angle between two lines is $\tan\varphi=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\dfrac{3}{1+4}=\dfrac35$, which is positive because the angle is acute. Check: $\arctan4=75.96^\circ$ and $\arctan1=45^\circ$, the difference is $30.96^\circ$ and $\tan30.96^\circ=0.6$. Negative options cannot be the tangent of an acute angle, and $\dfrac53$ is the reciprocal. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the differential equation $3\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x^2}+x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Divide by $3$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac13\left(x^{-2}+x\right)$. Integrate with respect to $x$: $\displaystyle\int x^{-2}\,dx=-x^{-1}=-\dfrac1x$ and $\int x\,dx=\dfrac{x^2}{2}$. Hence $y=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac1x\right)+c$. Check: $\dfrac{d}{dx}$ of the right side is $\dfrac13\left(x+\dfrac1{x^2}\right)$, and $3\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+\dfrac1{x^2}$. Option B loses the sign when integrating $x^{-2}$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A geometric progression has first term $16$ and sum to infinity $40$. The common ratio of the progression is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a convergent geometric progression $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$. So $40=\dfrac{16}{1-r}$, giving $1-r=\dfrac{16}{40}=\dfrac25$ and $r=\dfrac35$. Since $|r|<1$ the series converges. Option A is the value of $1-r$, not of $r$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The equation of a line is $\mathbf r=\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+7\mathbf k+\mu(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$ and the equation of a plane is $2x+3y-2z=5$. The sine of the acute angle between the line and the plane is

*Options as printed:* A) $\dfrac27$   B) $\dfrac37$   C) $\dfrac17$   D) $\dfrac57$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The direction of the line is $\mathbf d=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ and a normal to the plane is $\mathbf n=2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j-2\mathbf k$. The angle $\varphi$ between a line and a plane satisfies $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$. Here $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=6+3-4=5$, $|\mathbf d|=\sqrt{14}$ and $|\mathbf n|=\sqrt{17}$, so $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{238}}\approx0.324$ ($\varphi\approx18.9^\circ$). **Answer: $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{238}}$.** This value is none of the printed options ($\frac27\approx0.286$, $\frac37\approx0.429$, $\frac17\approx0.143$, $\frac57\approx0.714$), so the printed question is inconsistent (misprinted data or options).



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution set of $\dfrac{x+1}{x}\ge0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The fraction changes sign only at $x=-1$ (numerator zero) and $x=0$ (denominator zero, expression undefined). Sign table: for $x<-1$ both $x+1$ and $x$ are negative, so the quotient is positive; for $-1<x<0$ the numerator is positive and the denominator negative, so the quotient is negative; for $x>0$ both are positive, so the quotient is positive. The quotient is $0$ at $x=-1$. So $\dfrac{x+1}{x}\ge0$ for $x\le-1$ or $x>0$ ($x=0$ is excluded because the expression is undefined). Option A is the only option with this shape, although it writes $x\ge0$ instead of $x>0$. Option C is where the quotient is $\le0$, and options B and D include values such as $x=-\frac12$, where the quotient is negative. Multiplying by $x$ without considering its sign is the usual trap. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $4\cos\theta+3\sin\theta\equiv R\sin(\theta+\alpha)$, the value of $R$ and $\tan\alpha$ are respectively
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand $R\sin(\theta+\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\,\sin\theta+R\sin\alpha\,\cos\theta$ and compare with $3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta$: $R\cos\alpha=3$ and $R\sin\alpha=4$. Squaring and adding gives $R^2=9+16=25$, so $R=5$ ($R>0$). Dividing gives $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{4}{3}$ (with $\alpha\approx53.13^\circ$ in the first quadrant). Options A and C use $R^2=25$ as if it were $R$; options A and B swap the roles of sine and cosine in $\tan\alpha$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A circle with radius $4$ has its centre at the point $(2,4)$. The equation of the circle is
questions.corrige_markdown: The circle with centre $(a,b)$ and radius $r$ is $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$. With $(a,b)=(2,4)$ and $r=4$: $(x-2)^2+(y-4)^2=16$. Options B and D use $4$ on the right-hand side, which is the radius $r$ and not $r^2=16$; option C swaps the coordinates of the centre. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the equation $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The principal value is $\theta=\dfrac\pi6$ because $\cos\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Cosine is even and has period $2\pi$, so all solutions are $\theta=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6$, $n\in\mathbb Z$. Options A and C use $\dfrac\pi3$ (the angle with cosine $\dfrac12$), and options C and D use the period $\pi$ (which belongs to the tangent, not to the cosine). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $X$ and $Y$ are two variables related by the equation $Y=aX^2+bX$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. A suitable linear transformation for this non-linear equation is
questions.corrige_markdown: Divide $Y=aX^2+bX$ by $X$ (for $X\ne0$): $\dfrac YX=aX+b$. This is of the form $y=mx+c$ with the new variables $y=\dfrac YX$ and $x=X$: a straight line of gradient $a$ and intercept $b$. Option B is only a factorisation of the right-hand side, not a linear relation, and options C and D contain $\ln(aX+b)$ or $\ln(aX^2)+\ln(bX)=\ln(abX^3)$, which are not linear in the unknowns $a$ and $b$ (and the latter is not $\ln Y$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A partial order relation is that which is
questions.corrige_markdown: A partial order on a set is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive (for example $\le$ on $\mathbb R$, or divisibility on $\mathbb N$). Option A (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) defines an equivalence relation. Options B and D are incomplete and contain symmetry, which contradicts antisymmetry for a non-trivial order. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the parametric equations $x=2\theta+\sin2\theta$, $y=1-\cos2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the parameter, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Differentiate with respect to $\theta$: $\dfrac{dx}{d\theta}=2+2\cos2\theta$ and $\dfrac{dy}{d\theta}=2\sin2\theta$. Then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}=\dfrac{2\sin2\theta}{2+2\cos2\theta}=\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}$. This simplifies to $\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}=\tan\theta$ (numerical check at $\theta=0.7$: both give $0.8423$). Option B is $\cot\theta$, the reciprocal, and options A and C have a spurious minus sign (A also a wrong denominator). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $(1+ax)^{\frac12}\equiv1+\dfrac x2+bx^2+\cdots$,
questions.corrige_markdown: The binomial series gives $(1+ax)^{1/2}=1+\dfrac12(ax)+\dfrac{\frac12\left(-\frac12\right)}{2!}(ax)^2+\cdots=1+\dfrac{a}{2}x-\dfrac{a^2}{8}x^2+\cdots$. Matching the coefficient of $x$: $\dfrac a2=\dfrac12$, so $a=1$. Matching the coefficient of $x^2$: $b=-\dfrac{a^2}{8}=-\dfrac18$. Check: for $x=0.01$, $\sqrt{1.01}=1.0049876$ and $1+0.005-0.00001250=1.0049875$. Option C forgets the division by $2!$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word *ASSASSINATION* is
questions.corrige_markdown: ASSASSINATION has $13$ letters: A appears $3$ times, S $4$ times, I $2$ times, N $2$ times, and T and O once each. The number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{13!}{3!\,4!\,2!\,2!}=\dfrac{13!}{4!\,3!\,2!\,2!}=10\,810\,800$. Option A leaves out one of the repeated pairs (I or N), and options C and D start from $5!$, which does not match $13$ letters. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the sum of the first $n$ terms of a sequence is $S_n$, where $S_n=n(n+2)$, the fourth term of the sequence is
questions.corrige_markdown: The fourth term is the difference of two consecutive sums: $u_4=S_4-S_3=4(6)-3(5)=24-15=9$. Check with the general term $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=n(n+2)-(n-1)(n+1)=2n+1$, so $u_4=9$. Option A is $S_4$ (the sum of the first four terms) and option B is $S_3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The polynomial $p(x)=x^3+ax^2+2x-5$ leaves the remainder $2$ when divided by $(x-1)$. The value of $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $(x-1)$ is $p(1)$. So $p(1)=1+a+2-5=a-2=2$, giving $a=4$. Check: $p(x)=x^3+4x^2+2x-5$ and $p(1)=1+4+2-5=2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{100}(r+1)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Split the sum: $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{100}(r+1)=\sum_{r=1}^{100}r+\sum_{r=1}^{100}1=\dfrac{100\cdot101}{2}+100=5050+100=5150$. (Equivalently it is $2+3+\cdots+101=5151-1=5150$.) Option A forgets the $100$ added ones. **Answer: D.**

themes: division of a line segment in a ratio
questions.enonce_markdown: A point $P$ divides the line segment joining the points $(4,1)$ and $(5,2)$ internally in the ratio $2:3$. The coordinates of $P$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $A=(4,1)$ and $B=(5,2)$ with $AP:PB=2:3$. The section formula gives $P=\dfrac{3A+2B}{2+3}=\left(\dfrac{3\cdot4+2\cdot5}{5},\dfrac{3\cdot1+2\cdot2}{5}\right)=\left(\dfrac{22}{5},\dfrac75\right)$. Check: $P-A=\left(\dfrac25,\dfrac25\right)=\dfrac25(B-A)$, so $P$ is $\dfrac25$ of the way from $A$ to $B$. Options A, C and D forget to divide by $5$ one or both coordinates. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A periodic function $f$ is defined on $\mathbb R$, the set of real numbers, by $f(x)=\begin{cases}x+2,&0<x\le3,\\2x-13,&3<x\le5.\end{cases}$ If $f(x)=f(x+5k)$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, then $f(11)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The relation $f(x)=f(x+5k)$ says that $f$ has period $5$. So $f(11)=f(11-10)=f(1)$ (take $k=-2$). Since $0<1\le3$, the first rule applies: $f(1)=1+2=3$. Option B, $9=2(11)-13$, applies the second rule to $11$ without reducing the argument to the interval $(0,5]$, and option A, $13=11+2$, applies the first rule to $11$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of the constant $m$ for which the graph of the equation $y=m(x-2)^2+3$ passes through the origin $(0,0)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The graph passes through $(0,0)$ when $x=0$, $y=0$ satisfy the equation: $0=m(0-2)^2+3=4m+3$, so $m=-\dfrac34$. Check: with $m=-\dfrac34$, $y=-\dfrac34(4)+3=0$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: MECHANICS**

At time $t=0$ the position vectors of two particles $A$ and $B$ are $(5\mathbf i+20\mathbf j)$ m and $(-10\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)$ m respectively. The particles are given constant velocities $(-2\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $(3\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ respectively. The position vector of $B$ relative to the position vector of $A$ after $3$ s is
questions.corrige_markdown: With constant velocity, $\mathbf r=\mathbf r_0+\mathbf v t$. After $3$ s: $\mathbf r_A=(5\mathbf i+20\mathbf j)+3(-2\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)=-\mathbf i+5\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf r_B=(-10\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)+3(3\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)=-\mathbf i+10\mathbf j$. The position of $B$ relative to $A$ is $\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A=(-\mathbf i+10\mathbf j)-(-\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)=5\mathbf j$ m. Check with relative quantities: initial relative position $(-15\mathbf i-25\mathbf j)$, relative velocity $\mathbf v_B-\mathbf v_A=(5\mathbf i+10\mathbf j)$, so after $3$ s $(-15+15)\mathbf i+(-25+30)\mathbf j=5\mathbf j$. Option B is the position of $A$ relative to $B$; option C is the relative position at $t=0$; option D is the relative velocity. **Answer: A.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Two particles of mass $2$ kg and $3$ kg are placed at the points $(3,1)$ and $(8,6)$ respectively. The position of their centre of mass is at the point
questions.corrige_markdown: The centre of mass is $\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2}{m_1+m_2}$: $\bar x=\dfrac{2(3)+3(8)}{5}=\dfrac{30}{5}=6$ and $\bar y=\dfrac{2(1)+3(6)}{5}=\dfrac{20}{5}=4$. The centre of mass is $(6,4)$, closer to the heavier particle. Option B, $(5.5,3.5)$, is the midpoint, which would be correct only for equal masses. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is projected with speed $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at an angle $30^\circ$ to the horizontal through the point of projection. Taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the greatest height reached by the particle from the point of projection is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take upward as positive. The initial vertical velocity is $u_y=20\sin30^\circ=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At the greatest height the vertical velocity is $0$, so $0=u_y^2-2gH$ and $H=\dfrac{u_y^2}{2g}=\dfrac{100}{20}=5$ m. (Time to the top $t=\dfrac{u_y}{g}=1$ s and $H=10(1)-\tfrac12(10)(1)^2=5$ m.) Using the full speed $20$ in place of $u_y$ gives $\dfrac{400}{20}=20$ m, which is not the height here. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A lorry of mass $1000$ kg is moving with speed $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when a $200$ kg sack of rubbish is dropped vertically into the lorry. The new speed of the lorry is
questions.corrige_markdown: The sack falls vertically, so it has no horizontal momentum before it lands, and horizontal momentum is conserved (no horizontal external force). Before: $1000\times3=3000$ kg m s$^{-1}$. After: $(1000+200)v=1200v$. So $1200v=3000$ and $v=2.5=2\tfrac12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **Answer: B.**

themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics
questions.enonce_markdown: A body of weight $20$ N is suspended from a fixed point $O$ by a light elastic string of natural length $0.3$ m and modulus of elasticity $200$ N. The extension of the string is
questions.corrige_markdown: In equilibrium the tension $T$ balances the weight: $T=20$ N. Hooke's law gives $T=\dfrac{\lambda e}{l}$, so $20=\dfrac{200\,e}{0.3}$ and $e=\dfrac{20\times0.3}{200}=0.03$ m. Option B is the natural length, not the extension. (The body is assumed to hang at rest in equilibrium, as the question implies.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is projected from a point on a horizontal plane with speed $V$ at an angle $\theta$ to the plane. The horizontal range $R$ covered by the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown: The vertical motion $0=V\sin\theta\,T-\tfrac12gT^2$ gives the time of flight $T=\dfrac{2V\sin\theta}{g}$. The horizontal velocity is constant, $V\cos\theta$, so $R=V\cos\theta\cdot T=\dfrac{2V^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}=\dfrac{V^2\sin2\theta}{g}$. Option A has an extra factor $2$, and options B and C (which are equal, since $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$) are half the correct range because they lose the factor $2$ from $T$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two forces $\mathbf R=(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)$ N and $\mathbf F=(8\mathbf i+7\mathbf j)$ N act on a body of mass $10$ kg. The velocity of the body $4$ s after starting from rest is
questions.corrige_markdown: The resultant force is $\mathbf R+\mathbf F=(2+8)\mathbf i+(3+7)\mathbf j=(10\mathbf i+10\mathbf j)$ N. Newton's second law gives $\mathbf a=\dfrac{\text{resultant}}{m}=\dfrac{10\mathbf i+10\mathbf j}{10}=(\mathbf i+\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Starting from rest, $\mathbf v=\mathbf a t=4(\mathbf i+\mathbf j)=(4\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Option D, $40(\mathbf i+\mathbf j)$, forgets to divide by the mass (it is the impulse $\mathbf Ft$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force of $14$ N acts on a particle of mass $70$ kg causing the speed of the particle to increase from $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The distance travelled by the particle during this period is
questions.corrige_markdown: The acceleration is $a=\dfrac Fm=\dfrac{14}{70}=0.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (constant). Use $v^2=u^2+2as$: $49=9+2(0.2)s$, so $0.4s=40$ and $s=100$ m. Check with the work-energy principle: $Fs=\tfrac12m(v^2-u^2)$ gives $14s=35\times40=1400$ and $s=100$ m. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Fig. 1 shows two particles $P$ and $Q$ hanging freely and connected by a light inextensible string passing over a fixed smooth pulley.

![fig-1](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

(Fig. 1: $P$ has weight $20$ N, $Q$ has weight $30$ N, and the tension $T$ acts upwards on each particle.)

The system is released from rest. Taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the acceleration of $P$ and the tension in the string are
questions.corrige_markdown: The masses are $m_P=\dfrac{20}{10}=2$ kg and $m_Q=\dfrac{30}{10}=3$ kg. $Q$ is heavier, so $Q$ goes down and $P$ goes up with the same acceleration $a$ (inextensible string) and the same tension $T$ (light string, smooth pulley). For $P$ (upwards positive): $T-20=2a$. For $Q$ (downwards positive): $30-T=3a$. Adding: $10=5a$, so $a=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (upwards for $P$). Then $T=20+2(2)=24$ N. Check with $Q$: $30-24=6=3(2)$. Options A and C give $a=10$, the free-fall value; option B gives $T=20$, the tension when $P$ is at rest. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $4$ kg is moving in a horizontal circle of radius $2$ m. The centripetal force is $72$ N. The angular speed of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown: The centripetal force is $F=m\omega^2r$. So $72=4\,\omega^2(2)=8\omega^2$, hence $\omega^2=9$ and $\omega=3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Option C, $6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, is the linear speed $v=\omega r$, not the angular speed, and options C and D have units of speed instead of angular speed. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The position vector of a particle is $\mathbf r=\left[(t^3+2t^2+2)\mathbf i+(t^2-1)\mathbf j\right]$ m at time $t$ s. The velocity of the particle when $t=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Velocity is the derivative of position: $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=(3t^2+4t)\mathbf i+2t\,\mathbf j$. At $t=1$: $\mathbf v=(3+4)\mathbf i+2\mathbf j=(7\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Option C has the right $\mathbf i$ component but a wrong $\mathbf j$ component ($\dfrac{d}{dt}(t^2-1)=2t$, not $1$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The speeds of a car during $8$ s of braking are given in the table below.

| Time, $t$ s | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Speed, $v$ m s$^{-1}$ | 30 | 27 | 22 | 14 | 0 |

Using the trapezium rule, the distance covered by the car before coming to rest is approximately
questions.corrige_markdown: The distance is the area under the speed-time graph, $\displaystyle\int_0^8v\,dt$. There are $4$ strips of width $h=2$ with ordinates $30,27,22,14,0$. Trapezium rule: $\dfrac h2\left[y_0+y_4+2(y_1+y_2+y_3)\right]=1\times\left[30+0+2(27+22+14)\right]=30+126=156$ m. Check strip by strip: $\dfrac{30+27}{2}\cdot2=57$, $\dfrac{27+22}{2}\cdot2=49$, $\dfrac{22+14}{2}\cdot2=36$, $\dfrac{14+0}{2}\cdot2=14$, and $57+49+36+14=156$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The engine of a car of mass $1200$ kg works at a constant rate of $16$ kW. The car is moving on a straight level road with constant resistance of magnitude $400$ N to its motion. The maximum speed of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown: The power is $P=Fv$ where $F$ is the driving force. The speed is maximum when the acceleration is zero, so the driving force equals the resistance: $F=400$ N. Then $v_{\max}=\dfrac PF=\dfrac{16\,000}{400}=40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (convert $16$ kW to $16\,000$ W). The mass of the car is not needed (a distractor). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A fair die is thrown two times in succession. The probability of throwing at least one six is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use the complement: $P(\text{no six in two throws})=\dfrac56\times\dfrac56=\dfrac{25}{36}$, so $P(\text{at least one six})=1-\dfrac{25}{36}=\dfrac{11}{36}$. Check by counting: $6+6-1=11$ of the $36$ equally likely outcomes contain a six. Option A is the probability of two sixes, and option B adds $\frac{6}{36}+\frac{6}{36}$ without subtracting the outcome $(6,6)$ that was counted twice. **Answer: C.**

themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics
questions.enonce_markdown: The work done in stretching an elastic string of natural length $5$ m and modulus of elasticity $500$ N from a total length of $6$ m to $7$ m is
questions.corrige_markdown: The elastic energy stored at extension $x$ is $E=\dfrac{\lambda x^2}{2l}$ with $\lambda=500$ N and $l=5$ m. The total lengths $6$ m and $7$ m correspond to extensions $x_1=1$ m and $x_2=2$ m. The work done is the gain in elastic energy: $W=\dfrac{500}{2\times5}\left(2^2-1^2\right)=50\times3=150$ J. A common error is to use the total lengths $6$ and $7$ as extensions (that gives $650$ J) or to compute only the energy at the final extension ($200$ J). **Answer: C.**
